items.summary: Gemini spark on a space background
items.story_key: model:gemini|title:introducing tool retrieval in the gemini api
items.content_excerpt: Tool Retrieval is now in preview in the Gemini Interactions API. Load tool parameter schemas on demand instead of sending your full tool library in every prompt,designed to reduce input tokens and keep tool selection accurate as your agent scales. We are launching Tool Retrieval in the Gemini API to help your agents manage large tool libraries more efficiently. By loading parameter schemas only when needed, you reduce latency and input token costs for complex tasks. You can try this feature today in the Interactions API by adding a tool_search tool and setting defer_loading to true in your requests. We are introducing Tool Retrieval to help developers manage large collections of software tools more efficiently. Instead of loading every tool at once, your agent now keeps a library on standby and only pulls in the specific details it needs for a task. This reduces data usage, speeds up performance, and improves accuracy. You can start using this feature today with our latest Gemini models to build more capable and responsive applications. Today we're launching Tool Retrieval in the Gemini API, available in preview in the Interactions API . When an agent connects to dozens or even hundreds of tools, sending every full parameter schema on every request adds up fast. It inflates input token counts, adds latency, and lowers tool-selection accuracy as the candidate list grows. Tool Retrieval lets your agent keep its full tool library on standby and load parameter schemas only when the current task needs them. To turn on Tool Retrieval, add a tool_search tool to your request and set defer_loading: true on the tools you want to hold back. The model still sees the name and description of every deferred tool, so it knows what's available, but the parameter schemas stay out of context. When the model needs a tool, it asks for it by name, the API loads the full schema, and the model calls the function, all inside the same request. Inside that single API call, the model searches for issue_refund , the API loads its schema, and the model emits the function_call . All three steps appear in interaction.steps , making it easy to inspect which tools the model considered when debugging tool names or descriptions: From here it's normal function calling: your code runs the refund and sends back a function_result . There's no index to build or host. Gemini runs the search on the server, so the only changes to your code are the new tool and a flag on the tools you want to defer.

items.title: Introducing object enrichments: Transform unstructured data into agent-ready context
items.summary:
The vast majority of enterprise information is unstructured, locked away in object storage as petabytes of images, PDFs, videos, and audio files. This data holds the institutional knowledge AI agents need to do business-critical work. But to an agent, a raw object is just bytes it can't reason over. As enterprises start to deploy agents in production, the focus has shifted toward transforming these raw objects into rich, agent-ready context.

Today, we are introducing object enrichments, a new Google Cloud Storage capability that uses AI models to automatically extract rich contextual metadata from Cloud Storage objects and saves it in-place as object context, enabling agents to acquire the information needed to make complex business decisions. Object enrichments gives customers access to the AI models used by internal Google services such as Google Photos, offering image annotations like object detection and image labeling at 75% cost savings when compared to similar services from other cloud providers. Available in preview, this fully managed service also includes high-quality PDF classification model, enabling customers to seamlessly turn their object store into an intelligent, AI-ready foundation.

“L'Oreal is the 4th largest advertiser in the world, and managing media assets at that scale is complex. Cloud Storage object enrichments’s high quality and cost-effective annotations enable us to discover, understand, and govern our content at scale, accelerating marketing and advertising operations while remaining compliant in all markets. Object enrichments enables L'Oreal to label its extensive creative asset repository 100x faster at a fraction of the cost of existing pipelines and processes.” – Antoine Castex, Principal Data & AI Architect, L’Oreal

Agents need context, not raw bytes

To operate efficiently, agents need grounded knowledge; however, reading every raw file at scale is cost- and performance-prohibitive. For example, if an operations agent needs to pinpoint a specific event—such as a doorstep package delivery or a roadway hazard—streaming thousands of smart-camera or vehicle frames into the AI model on every user prompt would burn through expensive tokens and add minutes of delay. To bridge this gap, teams must pre-process raw data and extract rich, contextual metadata, which agents can then leverage at runtime. Historically, achieving this meant dealing with three challenges:

  • Cost: Running models over millions to billions of objects is expensive, pushing organizations to compromise and process only a fraction of their data, creating blind spots that lessen agents’ accuracy.

  • Operational toil: A self-managed pipeline means stitching together multiple services — from event triggers and queues to custom infrastructure built on Cloud Run or Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) — along with scalable retry/error logic and job scheduling. Once deployed, that infrastructure still requires continuous upgrades and capacity management. Teams sometimes spend months on this plumbing rather than focusing on building agents that solve actual business problems. 

  • Fragmented metadata: Extracted metadata often lands in a separate data store, decoupling context from the bytes it describes. Teams must pay for and maintain a second storage system, govern access policies across disconnected permission models, and run custom cleanup jobs to keep metadata in sync when source objects are copied, moved, or deleted.

This is why we built object enrichments: to natively provide agent-ready context for your unstructured data, equipping your agents with complete, grounded knowledge without prohibitive costs, custom pipeline plumbing, or fragmented metadata.

Key benefits of object enrichments

1. Reduce costs with Google models
Object enrichments offers dramatic savings at scale: enriching 10 million images or PDFs costs just $700 (according to published pricing). You can use Google’s high-quality AI models for image annotations—including object detection, face detection, image labeling, and explicit content detection—at one of the industry’s best price points. In addition, the PDF classification model lets you categorize documents into standard business and industry categories like Finance, Games, News, and Health.

"Even with a highly accurate baseline, Hyperscience leveraged object enrichments to drive a 50%+ lift in document classification accuracy, while simultaneously reducing classification inference costs by 2-3x.” – Mayur Pillay, VP Partnerships, Hyperscience

2. Generate richer context with Gemini
For complex multimodal reasoning across text, PDFs, images, audio, and video, you can leverage Gemini natively with object enrichments, unlocking advanced use cases such as summarization, entity extraction, transcription, and translation. Please reach out to us at storage-ai@google.com to learn more and request access to this upcoming functionality.

3. No pipeline, low toil setup
Skip the brittle, multi-component DIY pipelines. Setting up an enrichment job just takes three simple steps, with no code required in the Google Cloud console, or programmatically via the Cloud Storage API, following these steps:

  1. Define your scope: Provide a set of buckets containing the objects to process and specify the processing location. Object enrichments can scale to millions or billions of objects.

  2. Choose your models: Pick one or more of the five first-party Cloud Storage models for images and PDFs.

  3. Grant permissions: Grant the necessary IAM permissions to the object enrichments service to access your Cloud Storage buckets.

Object enrichments handles the rest: It orchestrates model inference, parses the responses, and writes the results to each object's object context, with built-in retries and throttling. There are no queues to manage, workers to scale, or glue code to maintain.

"Cloud Storage object enrichments and BigQuery, slashes AI development from 6 months to 1 month while rapidly improving our models." - Brandon Bunker, VP of Product AI, Vivint

4. Context lives where the bytes live
Instead of parking metadata in a separate data store, object enrichments writes model outputs directly to object context, a specialized Cloud Storage metadata construct that’s purpose-built for storing contextual information as structured key-value pairs alongside the object itself. Because context is stored alongside object’s actual bytes, you get enterprise-grade data management out of the box, with:

  • Cloud Storage durability and simplified lifecycle management: Object context shares the same durability and consistency properties as the underlying Cloud Storage object. It travels automatically with the object during copy, move, and replication operations and is automatically removed when the object is deleted — no more cleanup jobs!

  • Fine-grained IAM governance: Using IAM, administrators can control who can read, add, update, or remove object context.

  • Fast object filtering and serving: Applications can filter object listings directly by object context key-value pairs or read context metadata alongside objects, in order to serve richer experiences.

  • Turnkey multimodal analytics in BigQuery: You can easily configure your object context to natively flow into BigQuery via Storage Insights datasets, allowing data teams to run SQL analytics, build dashboards, and join unstructured file insights with structured enterprise tables, without writing a single line of ETL code.

What customers are building

Early customers are already putting object enrichments to work across key business scenarios:

  • Creative asset search and media archives: Marketing, retail, and media organizations manage petabytes of creative image assets, where finding a specific asset, e.g., "a red car driving at sunset" or "a vintage convertible in the desert during golden hour", requires rich semantic metadata. Object enrichments automatically generates descriptive labels in object context, which can then be indexed into a vector database or BigQuery to power accurate retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) applications and asset-discovery agents.

  • Automated trust, safety, and content moderation: Social platforms, marketplaces, and digital media pipelines scan millions of user uploads and supplier catalogs every day for explicit content. Historically, scaling this for every single upload has been cost-prohibitive, but not anymore. With object enrichments, you can process 10 million images for just $700.

  • Training data curation for frontier AI: Autonomous driving, smart home, and robotics companies capture hundreds of millions of raw camera and sensor files. They often need targeted data samples for specific fine-tuning scenarios, which make up only a tiny fraction of their corpus. By enriching raw captures in place with object detection and image labeling models and then querying the resulting metadata in BigQuery, ML engineers can pinpoint exact training cohorts in minutes rather than months.

  • Multimodal analytics: Combine insights from images and documents with structured business data to drive personalization, fraud detection, and trend discovery — for example, analyzing customer uploaded images of the product alongside their comments and recent sales data.

Get started with object enrichments

Object enrichments is available in preview today in the Cloud Storage console and through the Cloud Storage API. To get started, check out the following resources

  • Read the documentation: Learn how to configure an enrichments job and use object contexts.

  • Analyze in BigQuery: Set up Storage Insights datasets and query your enrichments alongside your BigQuery business data.

  • Connect your agents: Pair object enrichments and object context with the Cloud Storage MCP server to give agents secure, IAM-scoped access to your data and its context.

  • Review pricing: See Cloud Storage pricing for details.

  • Gemini enrichments: Reach out to us at storage-ai@google.com to learn more and request access to this upcoming functionality.

  • Start building: Head to the Cloud Storage console to enrich your first bucket in just three clicks.

items.title: RagHarnessDebugger: Jev-Guided Agentic RAG in Contract Inference Repair Auditing
items.summary:
Agentic systems using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) must repair their own answers by gathering more evidence, testing alternative policies and deciding if, when, and what repairs are needed. Yet how do we know if a system's repairs are working when metrics like accuracy can be misleading? We present RagHarnessDebugger, a framework that records every repair decision in a Jev-guided harness for contract inference and audits the record to facilitate complete debugging of all decisions taken during a RAG repair journey. RagHarnessDebugger checks that each trace is intact, that each validation applies to the candidate it is counted for, and which answers the acceptance rule can reach. We tested our approach on ContractNLI non-disclosure agreements with two reader models and a replication set of separate contracts. Our debugger's audit layer exposed failure patterns that were hidden under aggregate metrics, policies acceptance cost of repairs vs regressions and policy acceptance gap of 77% and 76% of available but unrealised repairs on development and replication sets. Our audit, together with a labeled error analysis and replay mechanism, allowed following the execution path all the way to the terminal decision - uncovering where missing repairs became lost. Our revised harness improved accuracy over the initial BM25-only baseline by 3.6 points on development contracts and 3.7 points on the replication set, and even improved our full contract access reference score by 1.1 on development and 2.4 on replication set. While our work here demonstrates how the debugger can conduct decision root-cause analysis for missed repairs, the true value lies with providing this debugger for judgment visibility serving continuous improvement of RAG decisions and their explainability.
  Keywords: agentic RAG, AI evidence repair, harness explainability, counterfactual replay, Jev, ContractNLI

items.title: Learning to Coordinate: LLM-Guided Workflow Evolution for Token-Efficient Red Teaming
items.summary: Automated red teaming is essential for identifying safety failures in large language models (LLMs), but its practical scalability depends on the resources required to discover those failures. Multi-agent systems can combine complementary capabilities, yet repeated planning, redundant exchanges, and ineffective information routing can make their coordination expensive. Moreover, a target model's response indicates the outcome of a test without identifying which collaboration decision should change. We present Learning to Coordinate (L2C), an LLM-guided framework that evolves an executable multi-agent workflow for each red-teaming case. L2C represents agent responsibilities, execution dependencies, and input bindings in a versioned graph, and associates each graph with records of the information actually delivered and produced. A controller trained through supervised fine-tuning integrates these records with target responses, evaluator verdicts, and remaining budget to retain the workflow, refine instructions, restructure collaboration, or lock further editing. This design connects feedback to explicit changes in subsequent execution while allowing a useful organization to continue without repeated controller intervention. The evaluation protocol covers HarmBench with three execution backbones and two target models, together with component ablations, dataset transfer, and evaluator checks. Across the six executor-target configurations, L2C improves ASR over EvoSynth by 1.4 to 4.5 percentage points while reducing mean online tokens by 35.6% to 37.3%. L2C connects adaptive collaboration to the resource requirements of automated security evaluation.

items.title: Jailbreak Detection on Large Language Models via Contrastive Prototype Structures
items.summary: Jailbreak attempts and harmful prompts remain a challenge for the safe deployment of large language models. We study whether contrastively learned representations can support safety detection without training an additional downstream classifier. We propose Jailbreak Detection with Prototype Inference (JDPI), which uses binary safety labels to construct harmful and benign prototypes and makes predictions from relative prototype distances. JDPI uses only binary safety labels for encoder adaptation, prototype construction, and validation. In our setup, it uses fewer labeled examples than the classifier baseline (Method A) by avoiding the separate split used to train the downstream classifier. Across four benchmarks covering different input formats, contrastive fine-tuning improves JDPI's detection accuracy by 9.1-18.0 percentage points. Using the same encoder, JDPI achieves slightly higher ROC-AUC on one benchmark and stays within 0.017 of the baseline across all four. With dataset-specific adaptation, JDPI exceeds the released Llama Guard 3-8B baseline by 0.173-0.310 in ROC-AUC across the four benchmarks. In multi-turn replay on TomGibbs, JDPI uses accumulated user history as the conversation unfolds, achieving higher conversation-level accuracy than when it uses the current turn alone. Across 12 directed transfers, JDPI outperforms the classifier by an average of 1.59 percentage points in accuracy, demonstrating stronger cross-dataset robustness.

items.summary: How FlyDSL MonoKernels keep agents responsive with high-interactivity decode in vLLM on AMD Instinct GPUs, using model-specific fusion, data-ready handoffs, and specialized-decode integration.
items.story_key: model:vllm|title:keeping agents fast high interactivity decode with flydsl monokernels in vllm
items.content_excerpt: Interactive LLM applications depend on low decode latency. A coding agent must finish generating its current action before it can call the next tool, so decode sits on the task’s critical path. Serving these workloads at low concurrency prioritizes per-user responsiveness over aggregate throughput. A decode step executes a chain of GPU kernels for operations such as projections, attention, and expert computation. At small batch sizes, many of these kernels do only a little work, yet each still incurs GPU-side dispatch, startup, and completion costs. A dependent kernel cannot proceed until its inputs are ready, so whole-kernel boundaries also limit overlap. Repeated across a long chain, these costs can account for a substantial part of decode latency, while the small amount of parallel work leaves GPU capacity unused. HIP graphs reduce CPU launch overhead, but do not eliminate these GPU-side costs. Figure 1 illustrates the repeated stages; widths and gaps are schematic, not measured durations or an overhead breakdown. This post explores how MonoKernels written in FlyDSL reduce decode latency in vLLM for interactive LLM serving on AMD Instinct GPUs. We explain the approach and its integration with vLLM, then examine performance and accuracy. A MonoKernel combines multiple dependent operator stages inside a single GPU kernel launch, using an explicitly designed schedule rather than a separate launch at every operator boundary. Here, mono means a single kernel execution boundary, not an entire model in one kernel. A model’s mono-decode path can contain several MonoKernels, and a decoder layer does not have to map to exactly one launch. The goal is not just to make individual operators faster, but to shorten the waits between them. Inspired by TileRT , the implementations discussed here use a persistent launch : a fixed grid of GPU thread blocks works through multiple stages. A thread block is a group of GPU threads executing together; it can continue with subsequent work once the required dependencies are satisfied. Both paths in Figure 2 can be replayed under HIP graphs. The difference is between multiple independent kernels and an author-designed persistent schedule within a launch. Some whole-kernel boundaries become finer-grained handoffs between portions of the computation. items.title: StitchRAG: Constructing Compact and Evidence-Preserving Contexts for RAG with Diffusion-Based Stitching
items.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves factuality by grounding large language models (LLMs) in external evidence. However, long retrieved contexts incur computational overhead and can even hurt performance due to noisy or irrelevant content. We propose \textsc{StitchRAG}, a framework for constructing compact context in RAG. \textsc{StitchRAG} builds a faithful, information-dense context while dynamically compressing the retrieved passages. We adapt the size reduction ratio to each passage by formulating a utility maximization trading-off the retained information and computation costs. We then extract answer candidates and query-related keywords from passages as anchors and collect passage sentences containing anchors under the derived size constraint. Finally, we connect or stitch the collected sentences together using text diffusion to form a coherent and natural context. Experiments on five open-domain QA benchmarks show that \textsc{StitchRAG} consistently outperforms diverse multi-step and compression baselines. Extensive ablations show the effectiveness of dynamic size allocation, anchor preservation, and diffusion-based stitching.

items.title: Hypnos: A Dual-Phase End-to-End Platform for Scalable Continual Learning at the Edge
items.summary: Continual learning (CL) enables neural networks to adapt to non-stationary data streams by mitigating catastrophic forgetting, offering a path to robust, private, and adaptable edge devices. Yet, porting CL to real-world edge devices remains challenging for two reasons: (i) online operation, where sensor data arrives one sample at a time and the device must adapt on-the-fly, and (ii) the low footprint of edge devices, which makes traditional error backpropagation training prohibitive. Inspired by the brain's wake and sleep cycles, the former for rapid adaptation with minimal resources and the latter for long-term consolidation, we introduce Hypnos, an open-source dual-phase platform for efficient CL at the edge. In the wake phase (e.g., daily operation), Hypnos relies on a low-footprint system-on-chip with a RISC-V microcontroller unit (MCU) targeting efficient inference and supporting lightweight gradient-free prototype updates. In the sleep phase (e.g., night-time charging), where wall-plug energy and larger memory budgets are available, a smart charger performs rehearsal-based gradient updates for consolidation. Deployed on a ZCU104 field-programmable gate array (FPGA) and synthesized in a 28-nm process, Hypnos is benchmarked on the CORe50 NICv2-391 protocol. It sets a new state-of-the-art accuracy of 78.6%-81.6% for edge CL systems, with an on-device latency of 7.79s-10.54s per sample depending on activation precision, and requires $3.8\times$ fewer learning steps and $22\times$ less learning compute than quantized latent replay at higher accuracy and comparable latency.

You pick a job, flip it to serverless, and then get hit with an error, an access-mode incompatibility, a Spark config that does not apply, a library that is installed on classic but not on serverless. items.content_excerpt: How Google DeepMind researchers built a new agentic framework that formally verified the code of Signal’s cryptographic protocol — long considered to be a grand security challenge Today, we’re sharing a milestone in software security long considered to be a grand challenge: Google DeepMind researchers guided AI agents to mathematically prove key security properties of the actual code underlying the Signal protocol, the technology that protects billions of private conversations in apps like Signal and Google Messages. This breakthrough discovery was made using AlphaProof Code , a novel agentic framework for formal verification at unprecedented depth that combines human expertise with AI agents. Formal verification—mathematically proving code runs correctly without flaws—is the highest standard of security assurance; however, it is difficult and often labor-intensive. Our work marks the first time AI has been used to formally verify a widely deployed cryptographic protocol at this depth. It's also the first time the implementation of a widely deployed protocol like this has been formally verified by any method, with or without AI. AlphaProof Code is a multi-LLM agentic framework that splits the work of formal verification the way a research team would: human experts work with AI to decide what to prove, and a group of AI agents does it. First, our researchers collaborated with a mix of models to translate Signal’s security goals into formal mathematical specifications, with human experts reviewing every one. From there, agents powered by Gemini Carbon did the proofs, generating over six million lines of Lean, a computer language that mathematically proves the accuracy of code. Next, the agents audited the proof and highlighted areas that needed a second look by a human – just one percent of the codebase, a massive time savings. Because Lean automatically checks the rest, our experts could focus their review where human judgment matters most. Cryptographic protocols underpin nearly all digital communication, from online banking to web browsing, and a single flaw can expose millions of people at once.   • Fixed the ? shortcuts list running its columns together in narrow terminals and being cut off at the bottom in short fullscreen windows
  • Fixed leftover hint text in screen reader mode on macOS and Linux after closing the /permissions search when the rule list was taller than the terminal
  • Improved Bash permission checks: some commands now ask first, or are refused where no one can answer
  • Improved permission checks in Code Mode; more sandboxed commands now ask or are refused
  • Improved the messages shown when Code Mode can't be turned on, so they say what you can do
  • Improved Bash sandbox protections on macOS, Linux and WSL
  • Changed edits in a session's mods folder to ask more often, and sandboxed commands to write to fewer folders; if every edit asks, remove any link there to an unreadable or network path
  • Improved Claude's sandbox instructions on Linux to explain that a server is reachable only from the command that started it
  • Improved how secrets are masked in push notifications from Remote Control and cloud sessions
  • Improved /logout and claude auth logout in the terminal to retry revoking the login, and to say where to revoke it if the server doesn't confirm
  • Improved Remote Control: replies from claude remote-control, Claude Desktop and VS Code sessions now stream to your phone or browser as they are written
  • Improved typing, streaming and resize responsiveness, especially in long sessions
  • Improved response time after reading or editing files, most noticeably on Windows
  • Improved idle CPU use: an idle session now wakes the machine less often
  • Improved CPU use when more than 20 subagents are running: token counts of background agents whose transcript isn't open now update every 5 seconds
  • Windows: Improved the speed of a session's first Bash command by about a second
  • Improved response time of the first message after /compact in git repositories
  • Improved response time in Claude Desktop for messages queued while Claude finishes a reply
  • Improved time to first response in Claude Desktop's new sessions: the first turn no longer waits up to 500 ms for local MCP servers whose tools load on demand
  • Improved how a PreToolUse hook's updatedInput is kept when more than one hook answers a tool call; the rewrite now runs in more cases
  • Improved the error when a PreToolUse hook exits 127, saying its check may not have run
  • Improved hook failures, blocks and timeouts in the transcript: failures are now red instead of grey, a hook that stops Claude is yellow, and the reason is shown under them
  • Improved the folder trust prompt, at launch and in /cd, to name the project settings files Claude Code will load; at launch it also marks files that run commands
  • Improved the folder trust prompt to say why Claude Code exited
  • Improved the message in non-interactive runs and background agents when a permission check fails with an error, so it names the cause
  • Improved Claude in Chrome permission requests from a terminal session over Remote Control: on claude.ai they now name the site Claude wants to act on, also when it is already allowed
  • Improved MCP tool errors in cloud sessions: when a call through the session's proxy is cut off after it was sent, Claude is told that the outcome is unknown
  • Improved /update-config in the terminal to use about 13,000 tokens of context instead of 93,000, and a rejected settings edit to quote only the changed settings
  • Improved Program Status Protocol (OSC 7501) reports: background commands, monitors and MCP tasks are listed, and a session waiting on them shows as working instead of done
  • Improved Monitor: when a watch expires with no events and its command wrote to stderr, Claude is now told so and told which file holds the output
  • Improved Claude in Chrome: a long browser_batch call now has 150 seconds to answer, up from 90, so fewer finished results are lost
  • Improved /doctor to share findings as it works instead of staying silent until the full report
  • Improved the error for a settings or .mcp.json file with broken JSON: it now gives the line and column
  • Improved commands that are off for your provider, sign-in or an environment variable such as DISABLE_TELEMETRY to say why instead of "Unknown command"
  • Improved the CERT_SIGNATURE_FAILURE connection error to name a possible cause after a CA renewal and what IT can change
  • Improved the message shown when a team's pooled group budget is used up: it now says when the budget resets
  • Improved the error shown when the API refuses a Console sign-in: it now says to run /login instead of pointing to an admin setting
  • Improved sign-in prompts: pasting a verification code or a web address now says what to do instead, and the prompt stays so you can paste the right code (#97)
  • Improved the /login screen: the code goes in a proper text field, a rejected code says why under it, and pasting in a short window scrolls the field into view
  • Improved /design-login, /install-github-app and MCP sign-in screens to match /login; the first two now mask the pasted code
  • Improved the Claude apps gateway sign-in screens: the sign-in address is a link and c copies it
  • Improved /plugin Discover and marketplace lists: they fit short windows with the cursor and key hints on screen, and Home, End, PgUp, PgDn, the mouse wheel and clicks now work
  • Improved /plugin Marketplaces and Add marketplace: a compact list, a clearer remove confirmation, a clear text field and shorter errors when adding fails
  • Improved /plugin Installed tab: Home, End, PgUp, PgDn and clicks now work, and hidden rows are counted
  • Improved /plugin Errors and Stats tabs: long errors no longer fill the screen, uninstalling from an error asks first, and long skill names no longer break the table
  • Improved claude plugin, mcp, update, doctor and auth logout output on a terminal to mark success, failure and warnings the same way (piped output keeps its old form)
  • Improved wording across the terminal: /plugin, /mcp, sign-in, setup, settings, the agent view, /teleport, Remote Control, update messages, spinner tips, /powerup and claude --help
  • Improved key hints in many dialogs and the ? lists: they show the keys that work, in one order and wording, and fit narrow windows; deeper screens in /hooks and /permissions say Esc goes back
  • Improved text fields in /add-dir, /export, /permissions, /feedback, /install-github-app and Bedrock and Vertex setup: one look, long text wraps, and a refused value can be corrected in place
  • Improved dialogs, panels and the transcript: errors, warnings and confirmations in many dialogs start with ✘, ⚠ or ✔, and loading lines, status rows, counts and durations look and read more alike
  • Improved long menus such as /permissions, /resume and /model to say how many rows are above and below, and the / and @ menus to count hidden rows outside fullscreen and screen reader mode
  • Improved list navigation: more lists wrap at both ends, checkbox lists in slash commands take Home and End, and /permissions says when a search finds nothing
  • Improved the pickers in agent view to take Home, End and paging
  • Improved agent view and the agent rows under the prompt to mark the selected row with the same pointer and color as other lists
  • Improved the footer after Ctrl+C stops background agents: it now offers ↓ to resume subagent while a stopped subagent is listed
  • Improved fullscreen mode: the prompt's borders now show how many lines of a long prompt are out of view
  • Improved /autocompact and /scroll-speed with a slider that shows every value, takes Home, End and (in fullscreen) clicks, and fits narrow terminals
  • Improved on/off settings to read on / off in /config, /memory and auto mode setup
  • Improved the send-now hint under queued messages: it now says "Queued" and no longer looks like part of your message
  • Improved terminal setup to list every change before making it
  • Improved alignment and spacing in /btw, /help, /scroll-speed, the settings error dialog and dialogs that suggest a plugin or setting
  • Changed terminal and VS Code sessions in organizations with the Claude Code + Cowork HIPAA configuration to start in auto mode by default; disableAutoMode turns it off
  • Changed terminal and VS Code sessions with no mode set to start in auto mode, not Manual mode, when your organization's policy hasn't loaded
  • Changed a managed-mcp.json added mid-session so it may apply at the next check; restart open sessions for it to apply in full
  • Changed Code Mode's $ shell helper to refuse some values with an error; nothing runs
  • Changed auto mode to stop some shell commands that ran before
  • Changed some Bash commands on macOS that ran before to ask or be refused
  • Changed a hook's "decision": "block" to hold in more cases, so a hook that always prints one may start blocking calls
  • Changed sessions that start in auto by default to take a server-managed defaultMode once settings load, or Manual if settings fail with no stored copy and policy fails or requires it
  • Changed auto mode for organizations with the Claude Code + Cowork HIPAA configuration: on a direct Anthropic API connection, the server-side classifier now checks actions, as for other organizations
  • Changed the Bash sandbox to keep its state in some cases during a session, until you run /sandbox or /cd; Bash may ask first
  • Changed sandboxed commands on macOS, Linux and WSL to no longer write to some sensitive home folders by default; some can be allowed with sandbox.filesystem.allowWrite in user or managed settings
  • Changed the Bash sandbox to set aside unexpected entries in a repository's .git folder after a command
  • Changed the Bash sandbox on Linux and WSL to create some missing --add-dir folders before each sandboxed command, so commands that create them can fail, skip, or land inside them
  • Changed commands that a permission hook or SDK host rewrites while approving to stay in the sandbox if the original was checked as sandboxed; the approver can add dangerouslyDisableSandbox: true
  • Changed claude mcp serve to ignore sandbox.excludedCommands
  • Changed /rewind on macOS, Linux and WSL to leave some files untouched and report them as skipped when the sandbox is on
  • Changed the Bash sandbox to ask before some lines that set environment variables when auto-allow is off; unattended runs can refuse them
  • Changed Claude's file tools to refuse writes to Claude Code's sign-in files, such as .credentials.json
  • Changed the Bash permission check to ask before more commands reach Claude Code's sign-in files
  • Changed some file tools to refuse some device and process files
  • Changed some cp and mv commands to ask first
  • Changed some tool calls in bypass permissions mode to ask for approval, or be denied where no one can be asked
  • Changed the Bash permission check to ask about some commands with very long values it can't finish checking, or to refuse them where a deny rule may apply or no one can answer
  • Changed subagents isolated in a worktree to refuse, in any repository, some git commands in Bash that can rewrite branches shared with your checkout; sessions are not affected
  • Changed ExitWorktree to refuse removing a worktree while a background subagent or shell command may still be running in it, unless Claude passes discard_changes
  • Changed the computer use macOS permissions panel to ignore j and k; the arrow keys and Ctrl+P/Ctrl+N still move the selection
  • Changed the PowerShell tool to ask before some more commands; unattended runs refuse them unless an allow rule, auto mode or bypass permissions mode allows them
  • Changed the PowerShell tool to ask about some more commands, even in bypass permissions mode, and to refuse some of them
  • Changed some malformed PowerShell commands to be denied
  • Changed some PowerShell tool commands that define a function named like a built-in command to be refused, so Claude can rename it
  • Changed auto mode to ignore some wildcard shell allow rules, such as ones that name no program or that start with $HOME, so the safety check decides those commands
  • Changed auto mode to judge wildcard allow rules whose program is a Windows backslash path, so those calls can be blocked; exact rules keep their allow; we plan to restore rules that start with .\
  • Changed a managed autoMode.environment list without "$defaults" to replace every built-in entry in Claude Desktop and Agent SDK apps too; add "$defaults" or copy the sensitive-target ones
  • Changed --add-dir and /add-dir in local terminal sessions to show the trust prompt for a folder you have not trusted yet; claude --bg refuses such a folder
  • Changed self-hosted runners under --trust-workspace false to ignore more repository settings; set such values in user or managed settings
  • Changed how permission answers over Remote Control and on self-hosted runners save "always allow" choices
  • Changed enabled plugins that were refused for a malformed plugin.json display field: they now load, with their hooks and MCP servers; administrators should check the plugins they deploy
  • Changed how allowedHttpHookUrls and httpHookAllowedEnvVars apply to hooks from managed settings
  • Changed HTTP hooks to ignore Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding in their headers setting; the request's length comes from its body
  • Changed plugin uninstall to also delete the files extracted from the plugin's MCP bundles (.mcpb, .dxt), unless another plugin uses the same bundle
  • Changed some worktree sessions to skip some plugin settings; a notice names what was skipped
  • Changed /plugin uninstall, remove and switch questions to lists answered with the arrow keys and Enter, or Esc to cancel; y, n and u no longer answer them
  • Changed automatic compaction in plan mode to use the model answering you, such as Opus with opusplan, so it can cost more
  • Changed Cowork cloud sessions to hold an organization's OpenTelemetry export until the first turn; a session that gets no message now sends nothing, so claude_code.session.count can fall
  • Changed Claude's messages to a session on another machine to be refused when your session uses an API key, auth token, profile or workload identity beside a saved claude.ai login
  • Changed --bare sessions on an unapproved API key: moving one to the background is now refused in most setups, and claude --bare --bg exits with an error if the background service lacks the key
  • Changed "Continue automatically at usage limit" to stop with a notice, sending nothing, when your login changes or ends during the wait
  • Remote Control: Changed how it connects through a proxy: requests now use a CONNECT tunnel, so a proxy that refuses CONNECT stops Remote Control with an error
  • Remote Control: Changed the session debug logs written under --verbose to go to ~/.claude/child-logs/
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed Linux and macOS sessions with no gh to get a built-in gh api by default, via Anthropic, which adds their GitHub sign-in, if any; --use-anthropic-gh false turns it off
  • Changed agent view so that quitting with Ctrl+C twice, Ctrl+D twice or /exit after pressing ← in an empty conversation ends that session, instead of leaving it running for 5 minutes
  • Changed --await-initialize to be refused with --bg or --worktree --tmux, which never read the initialize request, instead of starting without the fields it carries
  • Changed worktree creation, /teleport and IDE checkouts to run git with a stricter PATH; a git filter or helper may need its full path
  • Changed the card for approving a subagent's plan to two choices, "Yes, and switch to default (ask each time) for this session" and "No", chosen with the arrow keys and Enter (typed text moves to No)
  • Changed the /claude-api skill to build agents on Managed Agents by default, unless you want to host the agent loop yourself
  • Changed /usage in fullscreen mode to show plan limit bars before session cost for subscribers; /cost still starts with cost
  • Changed the wording of some messages that claude subcommands print; JSON output is unchanged
  • Changed first-run setup to preselect the "Auto (match terminal)" theme instead of Dark mode
  • Changed fullscreen /cd to refuse "Yes" while its trust prompt doesn't fit, with a line saying to make the window taller
  • Removed the tmux notice that said the mouse wheel needs set -g mouse on in fullscreen; the wheel scrolls without it
  • Removed the spinner tip that suggested /clear 30 minutes into a running turn
  • [VSCode] Added a claudeCode.promptSuggestions setting that turns prompt suggestions off
  • [VSCode] Fixed "Rewind code to here" in a forked conversation sometimes undoing one turn too many and deleting files created in that turn
  • [VSCode] Fixed the Sandbox dialog creating empty files and folders in the home directory and the project's .git folder while the sandbox is off
  • [VSCode] Fixed the saved sign-in being lost on some networks
  • [VSCode] Fixed sign-in ending when a verification code, a web address or a code from another sign-in attempt is pasted; the panel now says what to paste instead
  • [VSCode] Fixed the sign-in screen showing briefly each time a panel or window opened while signed in to Console without an API key
  • [VSCode] Fixed the usage-limit banner's "Request more" button for Team and Enterprise members coming back after each press without sending anything, after you signed in again during a session
  • [VSCode] Fixed /ide in a second Claude Code session silently losing the editor connection back to the first session; the newest connection now wins and the displaced session shows how to switch back
  • [VSCode] Fixed saved memories not being listed in the Memory dialog, or RAM use growing without end, when the memory folder held symlink loops, and a hang when it held a named pipe
  • [VSCode] Fixed a running command's live output stopping after one failed read
  • [VSCode] Fixed "Open in Terminal" showing only the shell's error when claude could not be started: in bash, zsh, fish and Git Bash, a notice now explains why and links to the install guide
  • [VSCode] Fixed the panel showing no "Open artifact" link after Claude publishes an artifact
  • [VSCode] Fixed the prompt suggestion hiding the "attach selected text" hint while the chat panel is unfocused
  • [VSCode] Fixed buttons with no visible border in the high-contrast themes, and the dark welcome art on the sign-in screen in Light High Contrast
  • [VSCode] Improved Edit and Write speed: no wait for new problems on files that are not open in a tab when the editor has been reporting none for such files
  • [VSCode] Changed a running command's live output in the chat to look like the command card's OUT row
  • [VSCode] Changed the text of extension errors in event listeners, views and activation to stay out of the editor's own error telemetry
